Save snippet as: 3002.1.3 Beeping Sound

The speed of a beep depends on the duration of both the sound and the pause between beeps. 

The example below beeps twice in 1 second (total duration of the 2 beeps is 1 second).


Make your robot beep 5 times in 1 second (no loops allowed).

Read up the Basic notes until 3003

Save snippet as: 3003.2.3 Soccer Scoring Board

In many applications, we need to control the layout of our display. Row and column are used to control the starting position of the text on the LCD.



Setting the LCD's Display Type to "On" is useful for displaying multiple LCD blocks together. Try out the following example.


            

Using LCD blocks, display the following Soccer Scores together for 3 seconds:

  1. Display "Team A" at the top left of the LCD.
  2. Display "Team B" at the top right of the LCD.
  3. Display "Score 1" at the bottom left of the LCD.
  4. Display "Score 5" at the bottom right of the LCD.

Read up the Basic notes until 3005

Save snippet as: 3005.1.5 Self Ordering Kiosk

Repeat While and Repeat Until are two conditional loops with the opposite meaning. This is how they work:



Below is an example of a condition. The condition is True if Button D22 is pressed (the value it returns is equal to 1)


You can make use of the following Wait-Until block, too. It will do nothing and wait until the indicated button is pressed or released.


You are creating a simple Self-Ordering program for a mini-fast food outlet. It will allow customers to buy burger or fries.


Create the program as follows:

1. Display "D18-start order" and wait until Button D18 is pressed and then released.

2. Repeat the following until Button D18 is pressed again:

  •   Display the choices.

  •   While Button D22 is pressed, display "free flow burger".
  •   While Button D24 is pressed, display "free flow fries".

3. Clear screen and end the program.

Use Repeat Until, Repeat While or Wait Until blocks in your code.

Your code may stretch out pretty far. You can change the layout for easier viewing.

Save snippet as: 3008.2.3 Polling Day

The example below shows a simple way of detecting what event has occurred by taking advantage of how fast a code is being executed.


You are creating a Voting program for your school Leadership Event.

      

Here's the flow of the program:

  1. Wait for voter to come.
  2. Wait for voter to choose.
  3. Check the voter's choice.
  4. The program will repeat for the next voter.

Create the program as follows:

1. Wait for voter to come.

  • Keep displaying "Step closer" until the Ultrasonic sensor value is less 20.

2. Wait for voter to choose.

  • Display the message below 
  • Wait until ANY of the following happens:
    - D22 is pressed
    - D24 is pressed
    - Voter walks away (distance > 20)

3. Check the voter's choice.

  • Display the message based on the following table

4. The program will repeat for the next voter.

Read up the Basic notes until 3010

Save snippet as: 3010.2.3 Remote Control

Create a program to control a robot car with the following features:

  • Press one button to steer left and another to steer right.
  • When no button is pressed, move forward. 
  • Press both buttons will reverse the robot.
  • If an obstacle is less than 5cm away, the robot will stop and can only reverse upon both button pressed.
  • You can decide the speeds and durations.
  • The program will keep running.

Put some obstacles around your robot and test it out.

Prioritise your features to see which should be checked first.

Read up the Basic notes until 3011

Save snippet as: 3011.2.3 Robot Server

We learnt earlier that we can plan our code by using Comment blocks to list down the sequence of actions.

After forming the sequence, we can start coding them in order. Below shows an example.


Note that it is normal that you may make amendments along the way.


You are building code to automate operations for your friend's restaurant using a Robot Server.


The code should work as follows:

  • The tables are marked with colour codes.
  • The robot will wait in the kitchen. When the food is ready, the chef will select the color of the destination table and press a button to send the robot out.
  • The robot will deliver the food to the correct table (based on its colour) and then return to its original position in the kitchen.

You got the idea and have to test it out using the virtual robot as shown.

   


Create the program using the flow indicated below as a guide.

Read up the Basic notes until 3012

Save snippet as: 3012.1.2 School Zone

When you need to compare many conditions, using nested if statements can be a more organized approach than joining them with multiple AND operators.

Consider the situation below:



An example of how you can implement the code is as shown.



You can also write it in these ways using Nested If (If block inside If block). 



Nested If statements allow you to check one condition first, and only if it is true, proceed to evaluate another. This can help make your code more organized and manageable in complex situations.


In Singapore, roads near schools are often painted red to alert drivers to slow down and watch for children. As a responsible citizen, you want your robot car to recognize school zones and adjust its speed automatically. You also want to add an auto-braking feature in your car when it detects someone close, especially when kids can dash across roads dangerously.

Create your program for the robot car as follows:
  • Travel at speed 40 in a normal zone and speed 10 in a school zone.
  • Steer left: Button D22
  • Steer right: Button D24
  • Moves forward: Buttons D22+D24
  • Brake when obstacle appeared less than 10cm away

Read up the Basic notes until 3015

Save snippet as: 3015.2.1 Game of Chances

Randomness is one of the indispensable features for game development because it gives an element of surprise. We learnt about the Random block that generates a random number. Below are some ways to use it.


Soon, you’ll learn about variables, which will allow you to check random numbers more effectively.


This is a game of chances. The idea is to select a colour and roll a random number to see if it is a match (1-Red, 2-Green, 3-Blue). The game will run 3 rounds to see if you can get it right 3 times in row.

     

Code the game base on the program design in the diagram.


You can design your own display format or use the sample shown below. Note that you must display user and robot choices when showing results.

    

Fun fact: Guessing a colour correctly has about 1-in-3 chance. Getting it right 3 times in a row? That’s less than 4%. Play your game and see who’s the super lucky one today!

1. You can use Nested-If to first check for robot's colour, then for user's colour.
2. Do it one part at a time. You can ask the instructor to check the flow.
